title: Knowledge Check 5: Lessons 33-40
description: Questions pooled from Lessons 33-40 of the salesforce-architect series. Score 80% or higher to progress toward the practice exam.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Bulkification & Trigger Frameworks: Limits-Aware Design That Scales”, a Bulk API load of 1,000 records hits an object whose trigger is already written for collections. How many times does the trigger execute, and why is each execution safe?
options: Once, because a single DML statement is one transaction with one governor budget.
Five times, because triggers batch at 200 records and each firing is a fresh transaction with its own governor budget.
Two hundred times, once per record, with the budget resetting on every firing.
Once per record, but all the firings share one governor budget.
questions.explanation: Triggers operate on batches of 200 records, so 1,000 records fire the trigger five times, and the design target is the spend inside one firing, not the spend across the load.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson’s guidance?
options: SOQL or DML inside a per-record loop makes resource use scale with batch size while the governor budget does not, so the query moves to an IN :Trigger.new bind and the DML becomes one call on a collected list.
A trigger that reads Trigger.new[0] is acceptable as long as the user interface usually saves one record at a time.
DML inside a loop is safe because each update call is cheap, and only SOQL counts against the statement budget.
Wrapping each record’s work in its own savepoint and rollback keeps a looped trigger inside its governor limits.
questions.explanation: Bulking the query and the DML into one call each makes consumption grow with the number of distinct objects touched rather than the number of records.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: Multiple triggers on one object are preferable because each one stays small and readable.
All of an object’s rules, DML, and validation should live in the trigger file so the logic is easy to find.
One thin trigger per object that routes to handler and service classes restores ordered execution and stops redundant queries from sharing the same governor budget.
A recursion guard becomes unnecessary once bulkification is done, because triggers batch at 200 records anyway.
questions.explanation: A single entry point per object keeps the firing order explicit, keeps one budget in view, and moves the logic into classes that a unit test can call directly.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Data Model Design: Inheritance, Polymorphic Relationships, and Denormalization Tradeoffs”, a support escalation must attach to an Account, an Opportunity, or a Case, and all three roll up to an Account in this org’s model. What does the architect do?
options: Remove the polymorphism and give the escalation a normal lookup to the Account that every candidate parent already has, keeping the relationship reportable and securable.
Build a custom polymorphic field so one field can point at any of the three objects.
Create three separate escalation objects, one per parent type, so every relationship stays simple.
Store a parent type and a parent Id in two text fields, since custom objects get no polymorphic field.
questions.explanation: The lesson’s honest move is to dissolve the polymorphism into an existing hierarchy rather than import a free-form field that every report, query, and sharing decision has to branch on.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson’s guidance?
options: Record types can hide a field from the database, so subtypes that need genuinely different fields should always be record types.
A record that legitimately belongs to two subtypes should be assigned both record types.
Roll-up summaries work across lookups as well as master-detail relationships, so the relationship type does not constrain the model.
When subtypes share almost nothing, separate subtype objects tied to a shared supertype are cleaner than record types, and the cost is that one roll-up can no longer count across all of them.
questions.explanation: Record types cannot hide a field from the database, only from the user, so deep divergence calls for separate subtype objects behind a shared supertype, which is exactly why aggregation across them needs more structure.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: Denormalization should be avoided entirely, because every stored copy is duplicated state.
A roll-up summary is platform-maintained denormalization that keeps the cached value current, but it requires a master-detail relationship and adds write cost on every child change.
A cross-object formula field stores its value and can be indexed, which makes it the faster option at high volume.
A hand-written trigger that maintains a count field is preferable because you control exactly when it updates.
questions.explanation: A roll-up summary gives a read without an aggregate query and the platform keeps the copies straight, at the price of a master-detail commitment, write cost on the parent, and a finite per-object budget.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Domain Modeling: Entities, Aggregates, and Bounded Contexts Applied to Agent Design”, a team is about to draw an agent graph for a claims intake system. What does the lesson say to draw first, and why?
options: The agent graph, because the tools actually available determine which responsibilities can be assigned.
A single agent covering triage, coverage, and adjudication, which the team splits later only if performance suffers.
The context map, because a bounded context is a conceptual boundary around a model while an agent is an implementation detail, and one context may use several agents.
The prompt library, because the vocabulary inside each prompt is what defines the boundaries.
questions.explanation: Do not equate agents with bounded contexts: the context map comes first, or the agent graph reproduces whatever tools happened to be available instead of the shape of the business.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson’s guidance?
options: The rule that an incident on a lapsed policy is not covered should live in the coverage agent’s prompt, because a model can reason about policy language.
The rule requires policy status, coverage dates, and the incident date to be read together, so it belongs in the aggregate with the policy as root and is checked only through the root.
The rule should be split across the triage and coverage tools so each one enforces the part it can see.
The rule should be enforced by the output schema, which is what typed contracts exist for.
questions.explanation: An aggregate is a consistency boundary, so anything that must stay true together is decided in one place behind the aggregate root rather than combined in free text by the agent.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: Treating model output as a proposal requires the model to be deterministic before the domain can authorize a change.
A bounded context and an agent are the same thing, so one agent should cover every context it participates in.
Model output is an untrusted proposal: constrain and parse it, normalize against trusted context, authorize deterministically, then execute through the aggregate that enforces the invariant.
Synonyms for one concept should be preserved per prompt so each agent can use the vocabulary its audience prefers.
questions.explanation: A schema can reject a missing field but cannot decide whether the user owns the claim or whether a date resolves correctly, so authority for the state change sits in deterministic domain code.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Sharing Architecture Deep Dive: Recalculation, Implicit Sharing, and When Sharing Can't Do the Job”, an architect changes a high-volume object’s org-wide default from Private to Read Only on a large org. What runs in the background?
options: Nothing; the flag flips and existing share records are left exactly as they were.
A one-time Apex managed sharing recalculation class, which the architect has to write and associate with the object.
A sharing recalculation that walks existing records and updates share records, and it may also delete shares that now grant no additional access.
A role hierarchy rebuild, because roles determine the default access level for an object.
questions.explanation: A recalculation is a cleanup pass as well as an expansion, so on a large object it is a scheduled event with a maintenance window rather than an impulse change.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson’s guidance?
options: If a user can see a child opportunity, case, contact, or order, they implicitly see the associated account, and the account hierarchy does not roll access up the way the role hierarchy does.
Implicit sharing applies to custom objects as well as standard parent-child pairings, and it can be disabled per object.
The account hierarchy rolls access up from a child account to its parent, exactly like the role hierarchy.
Implicit sharing is a configurable setting that an administrator turns on when parent access should follow child access.
questions.explanation: Implicit sharing is native and cannot be turned on or off, it only covers those standard parent-child pairings, and the account hierarchy is not a sharing relationship as the role hierarchy is.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: When certain users see too much, an additional sharing rule narrows their access back down.

Restriction rules are the declarative mechanism that narrows access, while Apex managed sharing is the escalation for requirements no declarative method can express, carrying a RowCause from a defined sharing reason.
A manual share survives a record owner change, which is why it is the right tool when an external system of truth drives access.
Apex managed sharing bypasses the sharing model and is recalculated separately from the rest of the org’s shares.
questions.explanation: Sharing rules and manual shares only ever open access, so genuinely private access is a restriction rule, and dynamic access that survives an owner transfer is Apex managed sharing.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Asynchronous Apex: Batch, Queueable, Scheduled, and Future, and How to Choose”, a nightly process must reconcile 40,000 Accounts against an ERP, retry failures on the next night’s run, and report a total. Which primitive and pattern fit?
options: A single @Future(callout=true) method that iterates all 40,000 accounts, because future methods run in their own transaction with a larger budget.
Batch Apex with a Database.Stateful counter and a status flag on each record so failed ones are picked up next run, kicked off by a schedulable.
One queueable job per account, enqueued in a loop, so each record’s retry is isolated in its own transaction.
A scheduled class whose execute method performs the reconciliation and the callouts directly, since scheduled Apex is asynchronous.
questions.explanation: Batch Apex is the primitive for volume and gives chunk-level fault isolation, a stateful counter carries the total across chunks, and the scheduler exists only to start it.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson’s guidance?
options: Enqueueing one job per record while iterating a 50,000-record query spends the shared 24-hour async ceiling in proportion to record count and hits the 50-job-per-transaction enqueue cap, so the work gets chunked before anything is enqueued.
Queueable jobs each run in their own transaction, so one job per record is the safest design for isolated retries.
Future methods are the better default for new work because they return a job Id that can be queried for status.
Because asynchronous limits are far higher than synchronous ones, the daily asynchronous ceiling behaves as a per-feature budget rather than an org-level one.
questions.explanation: The async ceiling and the per-transaction enqueue cap are both org-level, so a job per record multiplies the shared budget by the record count; chunk first, then enqueue.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: A schedulable should perform its own heavy queries and callouts, because scheduled Apex runs asynchronously and therefore gets asynchronous limits.
Batch Apex can call a future method from its execute method when a single chunk needs callout isolation.
Database.Stateful exists to carry large record collections between chunks.
Scheduled Apex runs under tight synchronous-style limits, so its execute body should be a one-line handoff that starts a batch job or enqueues a queueable.
questions.explanation: The scheduler holds the clock and nothing else: it hands off to a batch job or a queueable, which is where the higher asynchronous budget and the real work live.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Governor-Limit-Aware Design: SOQL, SOSL, and DML Budgets”, a loop updates one record per iteration and fails at the 151st record. Which meter fired, and what does the other meter show?
options: The DML row meter at 10,000 rows, with the statement meter already at its ceiling.
The DML statement meter at 150, while the row meter has barely moved, because one update on a collected list costs a single statement.
The SOQL statement meter at 100, because every update implies a query.
The query row meter at 50,000 rows, which no amount of batching can change.
questions.explanation: Statement count and row count are independent counters, and batching the same work into one DML call buys statement headroom, which is the scarce resource in a synchronous save.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson’s guidance?
options: 50,000 rows is the DML row ceiling, and it resets with each batch execute chunk.
Scheduled Apex gets the higher asynchronous budget: 200 queries, 12 MB of heap, and 60,000 milliseconds of CPU.
Moving to async roughly doubles the query and CPU budget and does nothing for DML, so a transaction failing on DML rows will not be saved by async alone.
A parent-child subquery inside a SOQL query is free, because it is part of a single top-level statement.
questions.explanation: Async raises query count, heap, and CPU, while DML stays at 150 statements and 10,000 rows and SOQL stays at 50,000 rows, so the meter that is failing decides whether async helps at all.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: The query and DML budget belongs to the transaction rather than to your code, so a design review asks who else touches this object in the same save and deliberately leaves headroom.
Certified managed packages share the org’s pool, which is why installing one can halve the available queries.
The 50 million row figure applies to any Database.getQueryLocator call, including one inside a synchronous transaction.
System.runAs is a test-only construct and does not consume DML statements.
questions.explanation: Everything firing on the save spends from one pool, so headroom and a budget sheet listing every consumer, including uncertified packages, are what keep a limit exception out of production.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Transaction Lifecycle: State, Save Order, and the 4 Trigger Contexts in One Transaction”, an after update trigger updates a field on the same record it was fired for. What does that cost and trigger?
options: Nothing extra, because after context writes to Trigger.new without spending a DML statement.
One DML statement, but the save order is not re-entered because the record is already in the database.
A DML statement against the transaction budget plus a full re-entry into the save order from step 1, which fires the record’s update triggers again.
An automatic rollback of the transaction, because an after trigger may not modify the record it was fired for.
questions.explanation: After context exists to touch records that need the saved Id or were not part of the original DML, and a write back to the same record restarts the sequence.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson’s guidance?
options: Roll-up summary fields recalculate near the end of the save order, after after triggers have run, so an after trigger that reads a parent’s roll-up is reading the pre-recalculation value.
Before triggers run after custom validation rules, so a validation rule can never see a value a before trigger set.
Values written to Trigger.new in a before trigger each cost a DML statement against the budget.
A workflow field update re-fires update triggers without limit, which is why the platform has to cap it at one extra pass.
questions.explanation: Roll-up recalculation happens well after after triggers, which is why sequencing bugs rather than logic bugs are the usual cause of a stale number.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: A record save that touches only one operation runs all four save contexts.

A batch that upserts 5,000 leads runs before insert, before update, after insert, and after update inside the single transaction, so insert-only logic misreads the updates as if they were new records.
Dispatching on System.TriggerOperation is discouraged in favor of chaining Trigger.isBefore and Trigger.isInsert checks.
An unhandled exception rolls back only the Apex work in the current phase, leaving the later phases to complete.
questions.explanation: A transaction is not limited to one DML statement or one operation, so a mixed upsert exercises all four contexts and a trigger has to dispatch on the operation type rather than assume it.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Stateful vs Stateless Agents: Context, Memory, and Tool State”, a B2B support agent asks the same qualifying questions on every contact, and a correction an expert makes mid-call disappears when the call ends. What is the architectural fix?
options: Increase the context window so the entire conversation history can be resent on every request.
Move state behind the API boundary: the client sends a message plus a session identifier, and the agent loads the relevant state and writes the updated state back.
Fine-tune the model on the correction so it persists in the weights.
Add more tools so the agent can look up whatever it needs at answer time.
questions.explanation: A stateless design pushes context selection onto the client and loses every correction at the end of the call, so the fix is a durable state layer the server reads and writes.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson’s guidance?
options: Context is what survives beyond the window, and memory is what is in the window right now.
A stateful agent is one giant record, so all durable knowledge belongs in a single store.
Consolidation is optional, because searching a pile of raw transcripts is as trustworthy as searching a curated index.
Semantic memory holds domain facts, policies, and durable knowledge and answers what is true, while episodic memory records time-indexed experiences and answers what happened.
questions.explanation: Working, episodic, semantic, and procedural layers hold different lifetimes and costs, and consolidation is what keeps the durable store small enough to retrieve from well.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: Because the attention budget is finite and recall degrades as context grows, an eviction and summarization strategy is non-negotiable, and tool output has to be designed for context efficiency.
Longer context always improves recall, so a model with a large window should be filled with as much history as possible.
Memory without grounding is safe as long as the store is durable.
One-shot extraction and classification tasks should be built stateful so they improve across requests.
questions.explanation: Context rot means longer context does not mean better recall, so something must always leave the window and the decision about what that is belongs to the architecture, not to the raw transcript.
